claim: MEF2C protein is enriched in NeuN-positive cortical neurons, with >99% of MEF2C-positive cells co-localizing with the neuronal marker NeuN.
source: Immunostaining of mature brain slices with MEF2C-specific monoclonal antibodies revealed that >99% of the MEF2C-positive cells co-localized with the neuronal marker, NeuN (Figure 1A), indicating that MEF2C expression in the cortex is primarily restricted to neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 1A showing co-localization of MEF2C and NeuN.

claim: MEF2C expression in the cortex is primarily restricted to neurons.
source: Immunostaining of mature brain slices with MEF2C-specific monoclonal antibodies revealed that >99% of the MEF2C-positive cells co-localized with the neuronal marker, NeuN (Figure 1A), indicating that MEF2C expression in the cortex is primarily restricted to neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the >99% co-localization data with NeuN, a neuronal marker.

claim: Emx1-Cre expresses in ~90% of differentiated neocortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons and in some forebrain glia starting as early as embryonic day 11.5 (E11.5).
source: To generate conditional gene disruption of Mef2c selectively in differentiated forebrain excitatory neurons, we bred homozygous floxed Mef2c mutant mice (Lin et al., 1997) with mice heterozygous for Cre recombinase inserted into the endogenous Emx1 gene (Iwasato et al., 2008), which expresses Cre in ~90% of differentiated neocortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons and in some forebrain glia starting as early as embryonic day 11.5 (E11.5).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iwasato et al., 2008.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice show selective and dramatic reduction of MEF2C protein levels throughout the cortex and hippocampus.
source: The Mef2c cKO (Mef2cfl/fl;Emx1IRES-Cre/+) mice show selective and dramatic reduction of MEF2C protein levels throughout the cortex and hippocampus, but no reductions were observed in the striatum or thalamus (Figure 1B) – Emx1-negative regions that express low levels of MEF2C.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No reductions in MEF2C protein levels were observed in the striatum or thalamus of Mef2c cKO mice.
source: The Mef2c cKO (Mef2cfl/fl;Emx1IRES-Cre/+) mice show selective and dramatic reduction of MEF2C protein levels throughout the cortex and hippocampus, but no reductions were observed in the striatum or thalamus (Figure 1B) – Emx1-negative regions that express low levels of MEF2C.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Striatum and thalamus are Emx1-negative regions that express low levels of MEF2C.
source: The Mef2c cKO (Mef2cfl/fl;Emx1IRES-Cre/+) mice show selective and dramatic reduction of MEF2C protein levels throughout the cortex and hippocampus, but no reductions were observed in the striatum or thalamus (Figure 1B) – Emx1-negative regions that express low levels of MEF2C.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data and knowledge of Emx1 expression patterns.

claim: Mef2c cKO offspring were viable and healthy.
source: The Mef2c cKO offspring were viable and healthy, and their body weights, growth trajectories and Mendelian frequency appear indistinguishable from their Cre-negative littermates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by observational data and body weight measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Body weights, growth trajectories and Mendelian frequency of Mef2c cKO mice appear indistinguishable from their Cre-negative littermates.
source: The Mef2c cKO offspring were viable and healthy, and their body weights, growth trajectories and Mendelian frequency appear indistinguishable from their Cre-negative littermates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and other unpublished data.

claim: Basal MEF2 transcriptional activity is reduced by ~35% in Mef2c cKO cortical neurons.
source: Using a 3XMRE (MEF2 response element)-luciferase reporter in cultured cortical neurons from control or Mef2c cKO offspring, we detected a ~35% decrease in basal MEF2 activity, but no deficit in depolarization-induced, MEF2-dependent transcriptional activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that MEF2A and MEF2D are sufficient to mediate normal levels of depolarization-dependent MEF2 activity.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mef2c cKO cortical neurons show no deficit in depolarization-induced, MEF2-dependent transcriptional activity.
source: Using a 3XMRE (MEF2 response element)-luciferase reporter in cultured cortical neurons from control or Mef2c cKO offspring, we detected a ~35% decrease in basal MEF2 activity, but no deficit in depolarization-induced, MEF2-dependent transcriptional activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that MEF2A and MEF2D are sufficient to mediate normal levels of depolarization-dependent MEF2 activity.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MEF2A and MEF2D are sufficient to mediate normal levels of depolarization-dependent MEF2 activity.
source: Using a 3XMRE (MEF2 response element)-luciferase reporter in cultured cortical neurons from control or Mef2c cKO offspring, we detected a ~35% decrease in basal MEF2 activity, but no deficit in depolarization-induced, MEF2-dependent transcriptional activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that MEF2A and MEF2D are sufficient to mediate normal levels of depolarization-dependent MEF2 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that depolarization-induced MEF2 activity is normal despite loss of MEF2C.

claim: Young adult Mef2c cKO mice exhibit normal gross brain morphology and cortical layer organization.
source: In young adult Mef2c cKO mice, we observed normal gross brain morphology and cortical layer organization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D), but Mef2c cKO mice did exhibit a slight decrease (~10%) in neocortical thickness compared to controls (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Nissl and NeuN staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice exhibit a slight decrease (~10%) in neocortical thickness compared to controls.
source: In young adult Mef2c cKO mice, we observed normal gross brain morphology and cortical layer organization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D), but Mef2c cKO mice did exhibit a slight decrease (~10%) in neocortical thickness compared to controls (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by cortical thickness measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Large reductions (~90%) in the frequency of spontaneous UP states were observed in acute slices from the somatosensory cortex of Mef2c cKO mice.
source: Surprisingly, we observed large reductions (~90%) in the frequency of spontaneous UP states in acute slices from the SSC of Mef2c cKO mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by UP state recording data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: UP states in Mef2c cKO mice were shorter in duration (~50%) and smaller in amplitude (~50%).
source: In addition, the UP states in the Mef2c cKO mice were shorter in duration (~50%) and smaller in amplitude (~50%) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by UP state recording data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Small decreases in both the frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) were detected in Mef2c cKO slices.
source: In the Mef2c cKO slices, we detected small decreases in both the frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) (Figure 2B), although the decrease in frequency did not quite reach statistical significance (p=0.07).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The decrease in mEPSC frequency in Mef2c cKO slices did not quite reach statistical significance (p=0.07).
source: In the Mef2c cKO slices, we detected small decreases in both the frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) (Figure 2B), although the decrease in frequency did not quite reach statistical significance (p=0.07).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Large increases in both the frequency and amplitude of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) were observed in Mef2c cKO slices.
source: We also observed large increases in both the frequency and amplitude of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Embryonic loss of MEF2C in cortical excitatory neurons results in a small decrease in glutamatergic synaptic transmission and a large increase in inhibitory synaptic transmission.
source: Together, these findings indicate that the embryonic loss of MEF2C in cortical excitatory neurons results in a small decrease in glutamatergic synaptic transmission and a large increase in inhibitory synaptic transmission – the combination of which likely contributes to the dramatic reduction in cortical network activity as detected by spontaneous UP states.
evidence: This is supported by the mEPSC and mIPSC data presented in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The combination of decreased glutamatergic and increased inhibitory synaptic transmission likely contributes to the dramatic reduction in cortical network activity as detected by spontaneous UP states.
source: Together, these findings indicate that the embryonic loss of MEF2C in cortical excitatory neurons results in a small decrease in glutamatergic synaptic transmission and a large increase in inhibitory synaptic transmission – the combination of which likely contributes to the dramatic reduction in cortical network activity as detected by spontaneous UP states.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined synaptic transmission and UP state data.

claim: Mef2c cKO cortical pyramidal neurons have normal dendritic complexity.
source: While the Mef2c cKO cortical pyramidal neurons have a normal dendritic complexity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), we detected a ~2-fold increase in dendritic GABAergic synapse density on Mef2c cKO cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 3A) as determined by quantifying co-localization of pre- and postsynaptic markers (GAD65 and GABRG2, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: A ~2-fold increase in dendritic GABAergic synapse density was detected on Mef2c cKO cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: While the Mef2c cKO cortical pyramidal neurons have a normal dendritic complexity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), we detected a ~2-fold increase in dendritic GABAergic synapse density on Mef2c cKO cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 3A) as determined by quantifying co-localization of pre- and postsynaptic markers (GAD65 and GABRG2, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A significant reduction in dendritic spine density was detected on Mef2c cKO neurons.
source: We also detected a significant reduction in dendritic spine density on Mef2c cKO neurons (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that MEF2C regulates, directly or indirectly, the densities of both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is supported by spine density measurements shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: MEF2C regulates, directly or indirectly, the densities of both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: We also detected a significant reduction in dendritic spine density on Mef2c cKO neurons (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that MEF2C regulates, directly or indirectly, the densities of both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed changes in both GABAergic synapse density and dendritic spine density.

claim: The direction of changes in E/I synapse density argues against the likelihood that the increase in inhibitory synapse density is a compensatory reaction to the reduction in excitatory synapse density, and vice versa.
source: The direction of these changes in E/I synapse density argues against the likelihood that the increase in inhibitory synapse density is a compensatory reaction to the reduction in excitatory synapse density, and vice versa, as these changes work in the same direction to reduce overall network synaptic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both changes reduce network activity rather than compensate for each other.

claim: Cre-expressing cortical pyramidal neurons displayed a significant increase in GABAergic synapse density.
source: Using this approach, we observe that Cre-expressing cortical pyramidal neurons displayed a significant increase in GABAergic synapse density (Figure 3C) and a significant decrease in dendritic spine density (Figure 3D), similar to the direction and magnitude of E/I synapse changes observed in the global Mef2c cKO neurons (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cre-expressing cortical pyramidal neurons displayed a significant decrease in dendritic spine density.
source: Using this approach, we observe that Cre-expressing cortical pyramidal neurons displayed a significant increase in GABAergic synapse density (Figure 3C) and a significant decrease in dendritic spine density (Figure 3D), similar to the direction and magnitude of E/I synapse changes observed in the global Mef2c cKO neurons (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by spine density measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: No significant changes in GABAergic synapse density were observed onto GAD65-positive Mef2cfl/fl interneurons transfected with Cre.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe any significant changes in GABAergic synapse density onto GAD65-positive Mef2cfl/fl interneurons transfected with Cre (Figure 3E), suggesting the increase in inhibitory synapses is specific to excitatory cortical pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The increase in inhibitory synapses is specific to excitatory cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe any significant changes in GABAergic synapse density onto GAD65-positive Mef2cfl/fl interneurons transfected with Cre (Figure 3E), suggesting the increase in inhibitory synapses is specific to excitatory cortical pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in interneurons compared to the increase in pyramidal neurons.

claim: Overexpression of MEF2C-VP16 in wild-type cortical pyramidal neurons significantly reduced dendritic spine density.
source: Consistent with this basic idea, we found that overexpression of MEF2C-VP16, a constitutively-active form of MEF2C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), in wild-type cortical pyramidal neurons significantly reduced dendritic spine density (Figure 3F), whereas a dominant-repressor form of MEF2C (MEF2C-EN) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) failed to alter dendritic spine density (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by spine density measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: MEF2C-EN failed to alter dendritic spine density in wild-type cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: Consistent with this basic idea, we found that overexpression of MEF2C-VP16, a constitutively-active form of MEF2C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), in wild-type cortical pyramidal neurons significantly reduced dendritic spine density (Figure 3F), whereas a dominant-repressor form of MEF2C (MEF2C-EN) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) failed to alter dendritic spine density (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by spine density measurements shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: Cell-autonomous expression of MEF2C-EN in Mef2c cKO neurons rescued the decrease in dendritic spine density.
source: However, cell-autonomous expression of MEF2C-EN in Mef2c cKO neurons rescued the decrease in dendritic spine density (Figure 3G), strongly suggesting that endogenous MEF2C functions as a transcriptional repressor to regulate dendritic spine density.
evidence: This is supported by spine density measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Endogenous MEF2C functions as a transcriptional repressor to regulate dendritic spine density.
source: However, cell-autonomous expression of MEF2C-EN in Mef2c cKO neurons rescued the decrease in dendritic spine density (Figure 3G), strongly suggesting that endogenous MEF2C functions as a transcriptional repressor to regulate dendritic spine density.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment showing that a repressor form of MEF2C can restore normal spine density.

claim: MEF2C-VP16 significantly increased GABAergic synapse density in wild-type cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: In wild-type cortical pyramidal neurons, MEF2C-VP16 also significantly increased GABAergic synapse density (Figure 3H), whereas MEF2C-EN had no effect on GABAergic synapse density (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemical analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: MEF2C-EN had no effect on GABAergic synapse density in wild-type cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: In wild-type cortical pyramidal neurons, MEF2C-VP16 also significantly increased GABAergic synapse density (Figure 3H), whereas MEF2C-EN had no effect on GABAergic synapse density (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemical analysis shown in Figure 3H,I.

claim: Cell-autonomous expression of MEF2C-EN rescued the increase in GABAergic synapse density observed in the Mef2c cKO cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: Similar to the dendritic spine density findings, cell-autonomous expression of MEF2C-EN rescued the increase in GABAergic synapse density observed in the Mef2c cKO cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemical analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Endogenous MEF2C functions predominantly as a transcriptional repressor to inhibit target genes that promote excitatory synapse elimination and inhibitory synapse formation and/or stability.
source: These results suggest that endogenous MEF2C functions predominantly as a transcriptional repressor to inhibit target genes that promote excitatory synapse elimination and inhibitory synapse formation and/or stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with MEF2C-EN and the effects of MEF2C-VP16.

claim: 1076 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were detected in Mef2c cKO cortex compared with controls using a stringent cut-off (|log2FC| > 0.3, FDR < 0.05).
source: Using a stringent cut-off (|log2FC| > 0.3, FDR < 0.05), we detected 1076 DEGs in Mef2c cKO cortex compared with controls, including 598 genes with a decreased expression level and 478 genes with an increased expression level.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: 598 genes showed decreased expression level in Mef2c cKO cortex compared with controls.
source: Using a stringent cut-off (|log2FC| > 0.3, FDR < 0.05), we detected 1076 DEGs in Mef2c cKO cortex compared with controls, including 598 genes with a decreased expression level and 478 genes with an increased expression level.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: 478 genes showed increased expression level in Mef2c cKO cortex compared with controls.
source: Using a stringent cut-off (|log2FC| > 0.3, FDR < 0.05), we detected 1076 DEGs in Mef2c cKO cortex compared with controls, including 598 genes with a decreased expression level and 478 genes with an increased expression level.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: The DEGs were highly enriched for neuron-expressed genes.
source: Comparing the Mef2c cKO DEGs to genes expressed in specific neuronal populations (Cahoy et al., 2008), the DEGs were highly enriched for neuron-expressed genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), consistent with the observation that Mef2c is not expressed at appreciable levels in non-neuronal cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cell-type specific gene expression data from Cahoy et al., 2008.

claim: The expression levels of Mef2a and Mef2d were not significantly altered in the Mef2c cKO mice.
source: Notably, the expression levels of Mef2a and Mef2d, which are close family members, were not significantly altered in the Mef2c cKO mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Genes with an increased expression level in the young adult Mef2c cKO cortex were significantly enriched for cellular processes such as neuron differentiation and development.
source: For instance, genes with an increased expression level in the young adult Mef2c cKO cortex were significantly enriched for cellular processes such as neuron differentiation and development, suggesting that MEF2C might function as a repressor for some of these DEGs.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Table 1.

claim: MEF2C might function as a repressor for some DEGs involved in neuron differentiation and development.
source: For instance, genes with an increased expression level in the young adult Mef2c cKO cortex were significantly enriched for cellular processes such as neuron differentiation and development, suggesting that MEF2C might function as a repressor for some of these DEGs.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of neuron differentiation and development genes among up-regulated DEGs.

claim: Analysis of down-regulated genes in Mef2c cKO mice revealed a significant enrichment for cellular processes including synaptic transmission and ion transport.
source: Analysis of down-regulated genes in Mef2c cKO mice revealed a significant enrichment for cellular processes including synaptic transmission and ion transport (p<0.01, BH correction; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting an important role for MEF2C in regulating synapse function and neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MEF2C has an important role in regulating synapse function and neuronal excitability.
source: Analysis of down-regulated genes in Mef2c cKO mice revealed a significant enrichment for cellular processes including synaptic transmission and ion transport (p<0.01, BH correction; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting an important role for MEF2C in regulating synapse function and neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of synaptic transmission and ion transport genes among down-regulated DEGs.

claim: A significant overrepresentation of ASD-risk genes was identified in the Mef2c cKO DEGs (p=0.0007, hypergeometric test, perm=0.001).
source: In the Mef2c cKO DEGs, we identified a significant overrepresentation of ASD-risk genes (p=0.0007, hypergeometric test, perm=0.001) and synapse-linked genes (p=0.0004, hypergeometric test, perm=0.001), (Figure 4B), including the autism-linked genes Ntng1, Nlgn1, Nrxn1, Nrxn3, Pcdh19, Shank2, Shank3, Pten and Htr1b.
evidence: This is supported by hypergeometric test analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A significant overrepresentation of synapse-linked genes was identified in the Mef2c cKO DEGs (p=0.0004, hypergeometric test, perm=0.001).
source: In the Mef2c cKO DEGs, we identified a significant overrepresentation of ASD-risk genes (p=0.0007, hypergeometric test, perm=0.001) and synapse-linked genes (p=0.0004, hypergeometric test, perm=0.001), (Figure 4B), including the autism-linked genes Ntng1, Nlgn1, Nrxn1, Nrxn3, Pcdh19, Shank2, Shank3, Pten and Htr1b.
evidence: This is supported by hypergeometric test analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The autism-linked genes Ntng1, Nlgn1, Nrxn1, Nrxn3, Pcdh19, Shank2, Shank3, Pten and Htr1b are among the Mef2c cKO DEGs.
source: In the Mef2c cKO DEGs, we identified a significant overrepresentation of ASD-risk genes (p=0.0007, hypergeometric test, perm=0.001) and synapse-linked genes (p=0.0004, hypergeometric test, perm=0.001), (Figure 4B), including the autism-linked genes Ntng1, Nlgn1, Nrxn1, Nrxn3, Pcdh19, Shank2, Shank3, Pten and Htr1b.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis and comparison to ASD gene databases.

claim: A significant enrichment for FMRP-associated RNAs was detected in the Mef2c cKO DEGs (p=3x10−07, hypergeometric test, perm=0.001).
source: We also detected a significant enrichment for FMRP-associated RNAs (p=3x10−07, hypergeometric test, perm=0.001), which is interesting since FMRP is required for MEF2C-VP16-induced excitatory synapse elimination (Pfeiffer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by hypergeometric test analysis and comparison to FMRP-target RNA databases.

claim: FMRP is required for MEF2C-VP16-induced excitatory synapse elimination.
source: We also detected a significant enrichment for FMRP-associated RNAs (p=3x10−07, hypergeometric test, perm=0.001), which is interesting since FMRP is required for MEF2C-VP16-induced excitatory synapse elimination (Pfeiffer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pfeiffer et al., 2010.

claim: Dysregulation of several Mef2c cKO DEGs was validated using quantitative PCR (qPCR) in both postnatal day 21 (P21) and adult SSC tissue.
source: Using quantitative PCR (qPCR), we validated dysregulation of several Mef2c cKO DEGs in both postnatal day 21 (P21) and adult SSC tissue (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Several dysregulated genes in Mef2c cKO mice are reported to regulate inhibitory GABAergic transmission (Gabra5 and Nos1).
source: Interestingly, there were several dysregulated genes that are reported to regulate inhibitory GABAergic transmission (Gabra5 and Nos1), and we observed a significant increase in Pcdh10 mRNA, a factor we previously implicated in MEF2/FMRP-dependent glutamatergic synapse elimination (Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq and qPCR data, and knowledge from the literature.

claim: A significant increase in Pcdh10 mRNA was observed in Mef2c cKO mice.
source: Interestingly, there were several dysregulated genes that are reported to regulate inhibitory GABAergic transmission (Gabra5 and Nos1), and we observed a significant increase in Pcdh10 mRNA, a factor we previously implicated in MEF2/FMRP-dependent glutamatergic synapse elimination (Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq and qPCR data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Pcdh10 is a factor previously implicated in MEF2/FMRP-dependent glutamatergic synapse elimination.
source: Interestingly, there were several dysregulated genes that are reported to regulate inhibitory GABAergic transmission (Gabra5 and Nos1), and we observed a significant increase in Pcdh10 mRNA, a factor we previously implicated in MEF2/FMRP-dependent glutamatergic synapse elimination (Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsai et al., 2012.

claim: MEF2C, either directly or indirectly, influences a large, complex gene expression program that influences neuronal and synapse development, and numerous syndromic and idiopathic autism-linked genes.
source: Overall, our RNAseq data analysis suggests that MEF2C, either directly or indirectly, influences a large, complex gene expression program that influences neuronal and synapse development, and numerous syndromic and idiopathic autism-linked genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-Seq analysis showing dysregulation of many genes involved in neuronal development and autism.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice displayed dramatic abnormalities in ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) produced by a young adult male mouse when placed in the presence of a female in estrous.
source: Mef2c cKO mice displayed dramatic abnormalities in a putative form of oral social communication in mice – ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) produced by a young adult male mouse when placed in the presence of a female in estrous or upon young pup separation from its mother (Figure 5) (Ey et al., 2013; Hanson and Hurley, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by USV recording data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the presence of a sexually-receptive female, Mef2c cKO males generated far fewer USV calls (~70% reduction).
source: In the presence of a sexually-receptive female, Mef2c cKO males generated far fewer USV calls (~70% reduction, Figure 5B), and showed a significant increase in the latency to the first call (~3-fold, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by USV recording data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mef2c cKO males showed a significant increase in the latency to the first USV call (~3-fold).
source: In the presence of a sexually-receptive female, Mef2c cKO males generated far fewer USV calls (~70% reduction, Figure 5B), and showed a significant increase in the latency to the first call (~3-fold, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by USV recording data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice produced a ~5-fold increase in unstructured USVs, and a corresponding decrease in complex, but not simple, USVs.
source: In contrast, Mef2c cKO mice produced a ~5-fold increase in unstructured USVs, and a corresponding decrease in complex, but not simple, USVs (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by USV analysis shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Significant reductions in the maximum USV frequency and the mean frequency at the end of calls were detected in Mef2c cKO mice.
source: While many basic USV parameters were unchanged by genotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F), we detected significant reductions in the maximum USV frequency and the mean frequency at the end of calls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is supported by USV analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–H.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice at postnatal days 4–10 produced significantly fewer USVs upon separation from the mother (distress calls).
source: Similar to the adults, Mef2c cKO mice at postnatal days 4–10 produced significantly fewer USVs upon separation from the mother (distress calls) (Figure 5D), but at this age, the USV structures, subtypes and basic call parameters were indistinguishable from WT littermates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–J).
evidence: This is supported by USV recording data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: At postnatal days 4–10, the USV structures, subtypes and basic call parameters of Mef2c cKO mice were indistinguishable from WT littermates.
source: Similar to the adults, Mef2c cKO mice at postnatal days 4–10 produced significantly fewer USVs upon separation from the mother (distress calls) (Figure 5D), but at this age, the USV structures, subtypes and basic call parameters were indistinguishable from WT littermates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–J).
evidence: This is supported by USV analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–J.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice produce significantly fewer USVs in a species-specific form of putative oral communication.
source: Together these data indicate that Mef2c cKO mice produce significantly fewer USVs in a species-specific form of putative oral communication.
evidence: This is inferred from the USV data in both adult and juvenile mice.

claim: Wild-type littermate mice spent significantly more time interacting with an unfamiliar mouse than an empty chamber in a social interaction test.
source: In a social interaction test, the wild-type littermates spent significantly more time interacting with an unfamiliar mouse than an empty chamber (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by social interaction test data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice spent more time interacting with the social animal vs. the empty chamber, but significantly less time interacting with the social animal than the control mice.
source: The Mef2c cKO mice also spend more time interacting with the social animal vs. the empty chamber, but the Mef2c cKO mice spent significantly less time interacting with the social animal than the control mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by social interaction test data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A significant reduction in social interaction was observed in Mef2c cKO mice even in the presence of a competing novel inanimate object.
source: In another cohort of mice, we observed a significant reduction in social interaction even in the presence of a competing novel inanimate object (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is supported by social interaction test data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1K.

claim: The reduction in social interaction in Mef2c cKO mice did not appear to be due to deficits in olfactory recognition of social animals or basic novelty detection.
source: The reduction in social interaction did not appear to be due to deficits in olfactory recognition of social animals or basic novelty detection, since Mef2c cKO mice showed a strong preference to interact with a social-related smell from an unfamiliar mouse (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is inferred from the social smell test data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice showed a strong preference to interact with a social-related smell from an unfamiliar mouse.
source: The reduction in social interaction did not appear to be due to deficits in olfactory recognition of social animals or basic novelty detection, since Mef2c cKO mice showed a strong preference to interact with a social-related smell from an unfamiliar mouse (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by social smell test data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice showed significant reductions in nest building.
source: In addition to social interaction deficits, Mef2c cKO mice showed significant reductions in another social-related behavior, nest building (Figure 5G) (Etherton et al., 2009; Kwon et al., 2006; Deacon, 2006), and they displayed abnormal social behavior in the tube test for social dominance (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by nest building test data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice displayed abnormal social behavior in the tube test for social dominance.
source: In addition to social interaction deficits, Mef2c cKO mice showed significant reductions in another social-related behavior, nest building (Figure 5G) (Etherton et al., 2009; Kwon et al., 2006; Deacon, 2006), and they displayed abnormal social behavior in the tube test for social dominance (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by tube test data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice show significant reductions in a hedonic-related behavior in the sucrose preference test.
source: Interestingly, Mef2c cKO mice show significant reductions in a hedonic-related behavior in the sucrose preference test (Figure 5I), an assay that measures an animal's preference for a sweet solution vs. water.
evidence: This is supported by sucrose preference test data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The reduction in sucrose preference in Mef2c cKO mice is not likely due to basic gustatory deficits since they showed normal avoidance of a bitter-tasting solution (quinine).
source: The reduction in sucrose preference is not likely due to basic gustatory deficits since Mef2c cKO mice showed normal avoidance of a bitter-tasting solution (quinine) (Figure 5I, right).
evidence: This is inferred from the quinine avoidance test data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice demonstrate multiple abnormalities in mouse social behaviors and a strong deficit in an appetitive reward-related behavior.
source: Taken together, Mef2c cKO mice demonstrate multiple abnormalities in mouse social behaviors and a strong deficit in an appetitive reward-related behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined behavioral test data.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice spent a significantly greater fraction of time in a repetitive jumping behavior (~3-fold increase).
source: Interestingly, Mef2c cKO mice spent a significantly greater fraction of time in a repetitive jumping behavior (~3-fold increase, Figure 6A), which was visually observed in both novel and home cage settings.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A significant increase in repetitive fine motor movements was detected in Mef2c cKO mice.
source: In addition, we detected a significant increase in repetitive fine motor movements (Figure 6B), which is often interpreted as a motor stereotypy behavior (Avale et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: No differences by genotype were observed in time spent self-grooming or digging in Mef2c cKO mice.
source: In contrast, no differences by genotype were observed in time spent self-grooming or digging (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice displayed normal motor coordination as measured in the accelerating rotarod test.
source: Mef2c cKO displayed normal motor coordination as measured in the accelerating rotarod test (Figure 6C), but significant motor hyperactivity was detected in a novel environment (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by rotarod test data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Significant motor hyperactivity was detected in Mef2c cKO mice in a novel environment.
source: Mef2c cKO displayed normal motor coordination as measured in the accelerating rotarod test (Figure 6C), but significant motor hyperactivity was detected in a novel environment (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by locomotor activity test data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Mef2c cKO and control littermates showed similar startle responses to a broad range of foot shock intensities and acoustic white-noise volumes.
source: Mef2c cKO and control littermates showed similar startle responses to a broad range of foot shock intensities and acoustic white-noise volumes (Figure 7A,B), suggesting that nociception and auditory sensory sensitivity are not significantly altered in the mutant mice.
evidence: This is supported by startle response test data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Nociception and auditory sensory sensitivity are not significantly altered in the Mef2c cKO mice.
source: Mef2c cKO and control littermates showed similar startle responses to a broad range of foot shock intensities and acoustic white-noise volumes (Figure 7A,B), suggesting that nociception and auditory sensory sensitivity are not significantly altered in the mutant mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar startle responses to shock and acoustic stimuli.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice showed profound deficits in threat-related learning and memory in the classic fear-conditioning assay.
source: However, the Mef2c cKO mice showed profound deficits in threat-related learning and memory in the classic fear-conditioning assay (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: This is supported by fear conditioning test data shown in Figure 7C–E.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice failed to develop robust freezing behaviors in the 1 min. periods following each tone-shock pairing.
source: Unlike the WT controls, the Mef2c cKO mice failed to develop robust freezing behaviors in the 1 min. periods following each tone-shock pairing (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by fear conditioning training data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Twenty-four hours after training, Mef2c cKO mice showed significantly reduced freezing behaviors when re-exposed to the shock-paired context.
source: Twenty-four hours later, Mef2c cKO mice showed significantly reduced freezing behaviors when re-exposed to the shock-paired context (Figure 7D) or after presentation of the tone cue (conditioned stimulus) in an altered context (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by contextual fear memory test data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice showed significantly reduced freezing behaviors after presentation of the tone cue (conditioned stimulus) in an altered context.
source: Twenty-four hours later, Mef2c cKO mice showed significantly reduced freezing behaviors when re-exposed to the shock-paired context (Figure 7D) or after presentation of the tone cue (conditioned stimulus) in an altered context (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by cued fear memory test data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Embryonic loss of MEF2C in excitatory forebrain neurons causes significant deficits in fear learning and memory, multiple social behaviors, socially-motivated ultrasonic vocalizations, and reward-related behaviors.
source: Together these findings suggest that embryonic loss of MEF2C in excitatory forebrain neurons causes significant deficits in fear learning and memory, multiple social behaviors, socially-motivated ultrasonic vocalizations, and reward-related behaviors.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined behavioral test data.

claim: Mef2c cKO mice show significant increases in repetitive motor behaviors and overall hyperactivity.
source: Mef2c cKO mice also show significant increases in repetitive motor behaviors and overall hyperactivity – all symptom domains with potential relevance to human neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism, ID and SCZ.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The behavioral phenotypes observed in Mef2c cKO mice have potential relevance to human neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism, ID and SCZ.
source: Mef2c cKO mice also show significant increases in repetitive motor behaviors and overall hyperactivity – all symptom domains with potential relevance to human neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism, ID and SCZ.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of mouse behavioral phenotypes to human disorder symptoms.

claim: Conditional embryonic deletion of Mef2c in cortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons (Emx1-lineage) produces a dramatic reduction in cortical network activity in vivo.
source: We show here that conditional embryonic deletion of Mef2c in cortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons (Emx1-lineage) produces a dramatic reduction in cortical network activity in vivo, due in part to a dramatic increase in inhibitory and a decrease in excitatory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is supported by UP state recording data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The dramatic reduction in cortical network activity in Mef2c cKO mice is due in part to a dramatic increase in inhibitory and a decrease in excitatory synaptic transmission.
source: We show here that conditional embryonic deletion of Mef2c in cortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons (Emx1-lineage) produces a dramatic reduction in cortical network activity in vivo, due in part to a dramatic increase in inhibitory and a decrease in excitatory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined UP state, mEPSC, and mIPSC data.

claim: MEF2C regulates E/I synapse density predominantly as a cell-autonomous, transcriptional repressor.
source: In addition, we find that MEF2C regulates E/I synapse density predominantly as a cell-autonomous, transcriptional repressor.
evidence: This is supported by the rescue experiments with MEF2C-EN shown in Figure 3G,I.

claim: Analysis of differential gene expression in Mef2c mutant cortex identified a significant overlap with numerous synapse- and autism-linked genes.
source: Analysis of differential gene expression in Mef2c mutant cortex identified a significant overlap with numerous synapse- and autism-linked genes, and the Mef2c mutant mice displayed numerous behaviors reminiscent of autism, ID and SCZ, suggesting that perturbing MEF2C function in neocortex can produce autistic- and ID-like behaviors in mice.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis and comparison to gene databases shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mef2c mutant mice displayed numerous behaviors reminiscent of autism, ID and SCZ.
source: Analysis of differential gene expression in Mef2c mutant cortex identified a significant overlap with numerous synapse- and autism-linked genes, and the Mef2c mutant mice displayed numerous behaviors reminiscent of autism, ID and SCZ, suggesting that perturbing MEF2C function in neocortex can produce autistic- and ID-like behaviors in mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: Perturbing MEF2C function in neocortex can produce autistic- and ID-like behaviors in mice.
source: Analysis of differential gene expression in Mef2c mutant cortex identified a significant overlap with numerous synapse- and autism-linked genes, and the Mef2c mutant mice displayed numerous behaviors reminiscent of autism, ID and SCZ, suggesting that perturbing MEF2C function in neocortex can produce autistic- and ID-like behaviors in mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral phenotypes observed in Mef2c cKO mice.

claim: An imbalance of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission in the brain is an emerging theory of the pathophysiology of multiple neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: An imbalance of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission in the brain is an emerging theory of the pathophysiology of multiple neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders (Garber, 2007; Zoghbi, 2003), including autism and SCZ.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garber, 2007 and Zoghbi, 2003.

claim: The genes and molecules that regulate the number of excitatory and inhibitory synapses formed and maintained on neurons remain poorly understood.
source: However, the genes and molecules that regulate the number of excitatory and inhibitory synapses formed and maintained on neurons remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: MEF2 transcription factor genes are expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons throughout development and adulthood in overlapping, but unique, expression patterns.
source: The MEF2 transcription factor genes are expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons throughout development and adulthood in overlapping, but unique, expression patterns (Lyons et al., 2012; Shalizi and Bonni, 2005; McKinsey et al., 2002), and they have been shown to regulate excitatory synapse density on multiple neuron types (Flavell et al., 2006; Li et al., 2008; Barbosa et al., 2008; Pulipparacharuvil et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lyons et al., 2012; Shalizi and Bonni, 2005; McKinsey et al., 2002.

claim: MEF2 transcription factors have been shown to regulate excitatory synapse density on multiple neuron types.
source: The MEF2 transcription factor genes are expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons throughout development and adulthood in overlapping, but unique, expression patterns (Lyons et al., 2012; Shalizi and Bonni, 2005; McKinsey et al., 2002), and they have been shown to regulate excitatory synapse density on multiple neuron types (Flavell et al., 2006; Li et al., 2008; Barbosa et al., 2008; Pulipparacharuvil et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Flavell et al., 2006; Li et al., 2008; Barbosa et al., 2008; Pulipparacharuvil et al., 2008.

claim: MEF2A and MEF2D can regulate activity-dependent elimination of glutamatergic synapses on both hippocampal pyramidal neurons and medium spiny neurons of the striatum in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: For example, MEF2A and MEF2D can regulate activity-dependent elimination of glutamatergic synapses on both hippocampal pyramidal neurons and medium spiny neurons of the striatum in a cell-autonomous manner (Flavell et al., 2006; Pulipparacharuvil et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Flavell et al., 2006; Pulipparacharuvil et al., 2008.

claim: Expression of a constitutively-active form of MEF2C (MEF2C-VP16) promotes excitatory synapse elimination in hippocampal pyramidal neurons in a complex process that requires the RNA-binding protein, Fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP).
source: Expression of a constitutively-active form of MEF2C (MEF2C-VP16) promotes excitatory synapse elimination in hippocampal pyramidal neurons in a complex process that requires the RNA-binding protein, Fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP) (Flavell et al., 2006; Pfeiffer et al., 2010; Tsai et al., 2012; Wilkerson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Flavell et al., 2006; Pfeiffer et al., 2010; Tsai et al., 2012; Wilkerson et al., 2014.

claim: Brain-wide deletion of Mef2c was reported to cause an increase in dendritic spine density on dentate granule neurons of the hippocampal dentate gyrus.
source: Brain-wide deletion of Mef2c was reported to cause an increase in dendritic spine density on dentate granule neurons of the hippocampal dentate gyrus (Barbosa et al., 2008), whereas another group reported that Mef2c deletion in embryonic neural stem cells (nestin-Cre), caused deficits in cortical neuron migration and excitatory synaptic transmission in a subset of animals (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barbosa et al., 2008.

claim: Mef2c deletion in embryonic neural stem cells (nestin-Cre) caused deficits in cortical neuron migration and excitatory synaptic transmission in a subset of animals.
source: Brain-wide deletion of Mef2c was reported to cause an increase in dendritic spine density on dentate granule neurons of the hippocampal dentate gyrus (Barbosa et al., 2008), whereas another group reported that Mef2c deletion in embryonic neural stem cells (nestin-Cre), caused deficits in cortical neuron migration and excitatory synaptic transmission in a subset of animals (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2008.

claim: Recent genetic studies have linked human MEF2C to a syndromic form of intellectual disability with autistic features.
source: Recent genetic studies have linked human MEF2C to a syndromic form of intellectual disability with autistic features, and single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) near MEF2C produce significant risk for SCZ (Paciorkowski et al., 2013; Mikhail et al., 2011; Novara et al., 2010; Le Meur et al., 2010; Cardoso et al., 2009; Engels et al., 2009), which highlight the importance of this gene for normal brain development and function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Paciorkowski et al., 2013; Mikhail et al., 2011; Novara et al., 2010; Le Meur et al., 2010; Cardoso et al., 2009; Engels et al., 2009.

claim: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) near MEF2C produce significant risk for SCZ.
source: Recent genetic studies have linked human MEF2C to a syndromic form of intellectual disability with autistic features, and single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) near MEF2C produce significant risk for SCZ (Paciorkowski et al., 2013; Mikhail et al., 2011; Novara et al., 2010; Le Meur et al., 2010; Cardoso et al., 2009; Engels et al., 2009), which highlight the importance of this gene for normal brain development and function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Paciorkowski et al., 2013; Mikhail et al., 2011; Novara et al., 2010; Le Meur et al., 2010; Cardoso et al., 2009; Engels et al., 2009.

claim: The functional role(s) of MEF2C in early neuronal development, particularly in the neocortex, remains unclear.
source: However, the functional role(s) of MEF2C in early neuronal development, particularly in the neocortex, remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: In the central nervous system, MEF2C is highly expressed very early in brain development (~E11.5), and its expression is enriched in differentiated forebrain neurons within the neocortex and dentate gyrus.
source: In the central nervous system, MEF2C is highly expressed very early in brain development (~E11.5), and its expression is enriched in differentiated forebrain neurons within the neocortex and dentate gyrus (Lyons et al., 1995; Leifer et al., 1993, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lyons et al., 1995; Leifer et al., 1993, 1997.

claim: Loss of MEF2C in forebrain excitatory neurons produces an increase in structural and functional excitatory synapses formed onto hippocampal dentate granule neurons (DG).
source: Loss of MEF2C in forebrain excitatory neurons produces an increase in structural and functional excitatory synapses formed onto hippocampal dentate granule neurons (DG) (Barbosa et al., 2008; Adachi et al., 2016), suggesting that MEF2C might have cell-type specific functions and/or that the increase in DG excitatory synaptic transmission is an indirect, homeostatic effect of decreased cortical stimulation of DG neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barbosa et al., 2008; Adachi et al., 2016.

claim: MEF2C might have cell-type specific functions and/or the increase in DG excitatory synaptic transmission is an indirect, homeostatic effect of decreased cortical stimulation of DG neurons.
source: Loss of MEF2C in forebrain excitatory neurons produces an increase in structural and functional excitatory synapses formed onto hippocampal dentate granule neurons (DG) (Barbosa et al., 2008; Adachi et al., 2016), suggesting that MEF2C might have cell-type specific functions and/or that the increase in DG excitatory synaptic transmission is an indirect, homeostatic effect of decreased cortical stimulation of DG neurons.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed differences between DG and cortical neurons.

claim: Postnatal Mef2c deletion in forebrain excitatory neurons did not produce social or repetitive behavioral phenotypes, despite the increase in DG dendritic spine density.
source: Also, postnatal Mef2c deletion in forebrain excitatory neurons did not produce social or repetitive behavioral phenotypes, despite the increase in DG dendritic spine density (Adachi et al., 2016), suggesting a dissociation of hippocampal DG spine density and postnatal MEF2C deletion from several ASD-related behaviors.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adachi et al., 2016.

claim: There is a dissociation of hippocampal DG spine density and postnatal MEF2C deletion from several ASD-related behaviors.
source: Also, postnatal Mef2c deletion in forebrain excitatory neurons did not produce social or repetitive behavioral phenotypes, despite the increase in DG dendritic spine density (Adachi et al., 2016), suggesting a dissociation of hippocampal DG spine density and postnatal MEF2C deletion from several ASD-related behaviors.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of behavioral phenotypes despite spine density changes.

claim: The role(s) for MEF2C in embryonic and/or early postnatal cortical development might be more critical for producing the behavioral phenotypes observed in Mef2c cKO mice.
source: As such, the role(s) for MEF2C in embryonic and/or early postnatal cortical development might be more critical for producing the behavioral phenotypes observed in our Mef2c cKO mice.
evidence: This is speculated based on the comparison with postnatal deletion studies.

claim: Imbalances in excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission are proposed to underlie many neuropsychiatric disorders, including ASDs and SCZ.
source: Imbalances in excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission are proposed to underlie many neuropsychiatric disorders, including ASDs (Rubenstein, 2010; Cellot and Cherubini, 2014) and SCZ (Coyle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rubenstein, 2010; Cellot and Cherubini, 2014; Coyle et al., 2016.

claim: Genetic analyses of patients affected by neurodevelopmental disorders revealed mutations in many synapse-related genes.
source: Genetic analyses of patients affected by these disorders revealed mutations in many synapse-related genes (Garber, 2007; McCarthy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garber, 2007; McCarthy et al., 2014.

claim: Increased excitatory synaptic function has been reported in several mouse ASD models, including mutant mice lacking Fmr1, Pten, and Tsc1/2 genes.
source: In mice, increased excitatory synaptic function has been reported in several mouse ASD models, including mutant mice lacking Fmr1, Pten, and Tsc1/2 genes (Gibson et al., 2008; Williams et al., 2015; Bateup et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gibson et al., 2008; Williams et al., 2015; Bateup et al., 2013.

claim: Mice containing a human disease mutation in the Nlgn3 gene (Nlgn3 R451C) displayed an increase in inhibitory synaptic transmission and several autism-associated behaviors.
source: For example, mice containing a human disease mutation in the Nlgn3 gene (Nlgn3 R451C) displayed an increase in inhibitory synaptic transmission and several autism-associated behaviors (Tabuchi et al., 2007), suggesting that altered E/I balance in either direction can produce behavioral phenotypes with potential relevance to neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tabuchi et al., 2007.

claim: Altered E/I balance in either direction can produce behavioral phenotypes with potential relevance to neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: For example, mice containing a human disease mutation in the Nlgn3 gene (Nlgn3 R451C) displayed an increase in inhibitory synaptic transmission and several autism-associated behaviors (Tabuchi et al., 2007), suggesting that altered E/I balance in either direction can produce behavioral phenotypes with potential relevance to neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both increased and decreased E/I balance can produce ASD-like behaviors.

claim: Little is currently known about the mechanisms that control GABAergic synapse density.
source: Little is currently known about the mechanisms that control GABAergic synapse density (Petrini and Barberis, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge, supported by citation to Petrini and Barberis, 2014.

claim: GABAergic synapse formation during development precedes glutamatergic synapse formation.
source: Interestingly, GABAergic synapse formation during development precedes glutamatergic synapse formation (Ben-Ari et al., 2007), and it can strongly affect the subsequent development of glutamatergic synapses and neuronal morphology (Wang and Kriegstein, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ben-Ari et al., 2007.

claim: GABAergic synapse formation can strongly affect the subsequent development of glutamatergic synapses and neuronal morphology.
source: Interestingly, GABAergic synapse formation during development precedes glutamatergic synapse formation (Ben-Ari et al., 2007), and it can strongly affect the subsequent development of glutamatergic synapses and neuronal morphology (Wang and Kriegstein, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang and Kriegstein, 2008.

claim: MEF2C in postsynaptic cortical neurons functions to cell-autonomously modulate the density of GABAergic synapses formed on the dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: Our finding here show that MEF2C in postsynaptic cortical neurons function to cell-autonomously modulate the density of GABAergic synapses formed on the dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the sparse Cre transfection experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Loss of MEF2C on cortical interneurons did not alter GABAergic synapse density.
source: In contrast, loss of MEF2C on cortical interneurons did not alter GABAergic synapse density (Figure 3E), suggesting a specific role in cortical pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Comparison of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the SSC of Mef2c cKO mice by RNA-Seq revealed ~1000 significantly altered genes.
source: Comparison of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the SSC of Mef2c cKO mice by RNA-Seq revealed ~1000 significantly altered genes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: Nearly half of the dysregulated genes in the Mef2c cKO cortex showed an increased expression level compared to controls.
source: Nearly half of the dysregulated genes in the Mef2c cKO cortex showed an increased expression level compared to controls, consistent with the idea that MEF2C can function as a transcriptional repressor, directly or indirectly, on a subset of these DEGs.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis showing 478 up-regulated genes out of 1076 total DEGs.

claim: MEF2C can function as a transcriptional repressor, directly or indirectly, on a subset of DEGs.
source: Nearly half of the dysregulated genes in the Mef2c cKO cortex showed an increased expression level compared to controls, consistent with the idea that MEF2C can function as a transcriptional repressor, directly or indirectly, on a subset of these DEGs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that many genes are up-regulated in the absence of MEF2C.

claim: Reduced Cdkl5 expression was found in the MEF2C cKO DEGs, consistent with the reduced expression of CDKL5 mRNA reported in human patients with MEF2C mutations.
source: Additionally, we found reduced Cdkl5 expression in the MEF2C cKO DEGs, consistent with the reduced expression of CDKL5 mRNA reported in human patients with MEF2C mutations (Zweier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data and citation to Zweier et al., 2010.

claim: Deletion of, or non-synonymous mutations in, the MEF2C gene is associated with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with features of autism and ID.
source: Recent human genetic studies have revealed that deletion of, or non-synonymous mutations in, the MEF2C gene is associated with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with features of autism and ID (Paciorkowski et al., 2013; Mikhail et al., 2011; Novara et al., 2010; Le Meur et al., 2010; Cardoso et al., 2009; Engels et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Paciorkowski et al., 2013; Mikhail et al., 2011; Novara et al., 2010; Le Meur et al., 2010; Cardoso et al., 2009; Engels et al., 2009.

claim: MEF2C haploinsufficient patients present with motor abnormalities (e.g. dyskinesias, stereotypies and hyperactivity), impairments in reciprocity, severe deficits in verbal communication, and severe intellectual disability.
source: These MEF2C haploinsufficient patients present with a number of symptoms, including motor abnormalities (e.g. dyskinesias, stereotypies and hyperactivity), impairments in reciprocity, severe deficits in verbal communication, and severe intellectual disability (Paciorkowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Paciorkowski et al., 2013.

claim: In humans, MEF2C haploinsufficiency appears to be sufficient, at least in reported individuals, to produce a complex and severe neurodevelopmental disorder.
source: In humans, MEF2C haploinsufficiency appears to be sufficient, at least in reported individuals, to produce this complex and severe neurodevelopmental disorder.
evidence: This is based on human genetic studies cited earlier.

claim: Loss of one gene copy of Mef2c (Mef2cfl/+;Emx1Cre/+) in the Emx1-cell lineage produces mice with behaviors indistinguishable from their Cre-negative WT controls.
source: Generally consistent with previous reports (Li et al., 2008; Barbosa et al., 2008), our preliminary studies indicate that loss of one gene copy of Mef2c (Mef2cfl/+;Emx1Cre/+) in the Emx1-cell lineage produces mice with behaviors indistinguishable from their Cre-negative WT controls (A.J.H. and C.W.C., unpublished observations).
evidence: This is supported by unpublished observations and citations to Li et al., 2008; Barbosa et al., 2008.

claim: In humans there may be other factors that influence disease penetrance and severity, including unique or sensitized functions for MEF2C through human evolution, human-specific genetic modifiers and/or environmental influences.
source: It is possible that in humans there are other factors that influence disease penetrance and severity, including unique or sensitized functions for MEF2C through human evolution, human-specific genetic modifiers and/or environmental influences that increase symptom penetrance or additional cell populations where reduction in MEF2C is required.
evidence: This is speculated to explain the difference between mouse and human phenotypes.

claim: MEF2C plays an essential role in early cortical synaptic development.
source: Nevertheless, our findings here indicate that MEF2C plays an essential role in early cortical synaptic development, and that reduction in MEF2C function in forebrain excitatory neurons can produce behaviors potentially relevant to multiple intellectual and developmental disorders.
evidence: This is supported by the synaptic phenotypes observed in Mef2c cKO mice.

claim: Reduction in MEF2C function in forebrain excitatory neurons can produce behaviors potentially relevant to multiple intellectual and developmental disorders.
source: Nevertheless, our findings here indicate that MEF2C plays an essential role in early cortical synaptic development, and that reduction in MEF2C function in forebrain excitatory neurons can produce behaviors potentially relevant to multiple intellectual and developmental disorders.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral phenotypes observed in Mef2c cKO mice.

claim: Schizophrenia is a debilitating mental illness with neurodevelopmental origins that affects nearly 1% of the world's population.
source: Schizophrenia is a debilitating mental illness with neurodevelopmental origins that affects nearly 1% of the world's population, and there is significant overlap in risk genes for ASDs and SCZ.
evidence: This is established knowledge about schizophrenia.

claim: There is significant overlap in risk genes for ASDs and SCZ.
source: Schizophrenia is a debilitating mental illness with neurodevelopmental origins that affects nearly 1% of the world's population, and there is significant overlap in risk genes for ASDs and SCZ.
evidence: This is established knowledge from genetic studies.

claim: Human postmortem brain analysis of SCZ brains revealed a thinning of the cortex and a decrease in dendritic spine density.
source: In contrast to ASDs, human postmortem brain analysis of SCZ brains revealed a thinning of the cortex and a decrease in dendritic spine density, observations supporting the leading hypothesis that hypofunction of excitatory synaptic transmission underlies the pathophysiology of SCZ (Coyle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coyle et al., 2016.

claim: Hypofunction of excitatory synaptic transmission underlies the pathophysiology of SCZ.
source: In contrast to ASDs, human postmortem brain analysis of SCZ brains revealed a thinning of the cortex and a decrease in dendritic spine density, observations supporting the leading hypothesis that hypofunction of excitatory synaptic transmission underlies the pathophysiology of SCZ (Coyle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a leading hypothesis supported by citation to Coyle et al., 2016.

claim: 108 genomic loci were identified by SNP meta-analysis as conferring significant risk for SCZ, and MEF2C was identified as a candidate risk gene.
source: Recently, 108 genomic loci were identified by SNP meta-analysis as conferring significant risk for SCZ, and MEF2C was identified as a candidate risk gene (Schizophrenia Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schizophrenia Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2014.

claim: In the Mef2c cKO mice, a thinning of the cortex was observed.
source: In the Mef2c cKO mice, we observed a thinning of the cortex (Figure 1C), a decrease in dendritic spine density of Mef2c cKO cortical neurons (Figure 3B), and behavioral phenotypes that are reminiscent of cognitive and negative symptoms of SCZ (e.g. learning and memory deficits, lack of pleasure and motivation, reduced sociability and poverty of speech).
evidence: This is supported by cortical thickness measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Behavioral phenotypes in Mef2c cKO mice are reminiscent of cognitive and negative symptoms of SCZ (e.g. learning and memory deficits, lack of pleasure and motivation, reduced sociability and poverty of speech).
source: In the Mef2c cKO mice, we observed a thinning of the cortex (Figure 1C), a decrease in dendritic spine density of Mef2c cKO cortical neurons (Figure 3B), and behavioral phenotypes that are reminiscent of cognitive and negative symptoms of SCZ (e.g. learning and memory deficits, lack of pleasure and motivation, reduced sociability and poverty of speech).
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral test data shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: Mef2c is required for proper synapse development on excitatory forebrain neurons.
source: In summary, we show here that Mef2c is required for proper synapse development on excitatory forebrain neurons, and its embryonic loss in these populations produces mice with behavior phenotypes reminiscent of multiple neurodevelopmental disorders, including ASDs and ID.
evidence: This is supported by the synaptic phenotypes observed in Mef2c cKO mice.

claim: Mef2c loss-of-function in Emx1-lineage populations produces, directly or indirectly, a dramatic dysregulation of hundreds of neuronal genes.
source: We also show that MEF2C likely regulates E/I synapse density by functioning as a cell-autonomous, transcriptional repressor, and that Mef2c loss-of-function in Emx1-lineage populations produces, directly or indirectly, a dramatic dysregulation of hundreds of neuronal genes, positioning it at the nexus of numerous critical neurodevelopment genes reported to influence neuronal and synaptic development and risk for neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis showing 1076 DEGs.
